Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. We said both in the same breath, every household under our catechism speaking the same words each week: conceived by the Holy Spirit, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. Not one nature or the other. Both, held together, never separated.

He is what we had of God's own speech - the Word, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture. We did not invent this and we did not discover it freshly ourselves; it reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone, our founder said: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. We confessed him, we did not prove him - the confession itself is what we have, not an argument built for a doubter from witnesses we ourselves could name.

To us he is Lord - each of us says my Lord, not only our Lord - the one Mediator between us and God, the one High Priest who stands for us. He redeemed us, a lost and condemned people, bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power, and it cost him his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. At our table his body and blood are truly present, in and under the bread and wine, and we take him at his word rather than explain the how.

The Word -- his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture. We did not invent it and we did not discover it freshly ourselves; it reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone, our own founder says: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. Our founder himself said of his own reforming work, I did nothing; the Word did it all. Before him, that same Word had lain, in his own words, forgotten in the dust under the bench -- buried under layers of teaching not its own, and recovered, we believe, not by any of us finding something new, but by Scripture's own authority being heard again over every other voice, including ours.

Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. We do not pretend otherwise. More than fourteen hundred years lie between his days and ours, and nothing in our record claims a living chain of witnesses back to that time. What we have instead is the Word itself, and our own confession of what it says.

By what path did it arrive? Through the ordinary mechanisms of the church before us -- copied, carried, argued over, taught. We did not claim a new channel or a new discovery. We claimed that what had always been there had been read rightly again.

I cannot set myself up as judge of any person's conscience - that is not what this office is - so I will not answer you with a verdict on what you have just named. What I can do is hand you what we held, plainly, and let it sit where it may.

We say that faith is not something you manufacture by effort, the way you might build a chair or master a trade. It is trust that holds onto a promise spoken from outside yourself - conceived from hearing the Word, never produced by your own strength. That Word is what we had of Jesus: his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture, preached, printed, and taught - not invented by us, and not discovered freshly by anyone's own cleverness. Our founder himself said plainly, I did nothing; the Word did it all. The promise never forces itself on anyone, and we do not compel a conscience toward it - only the free things may be pressed, and never past what love for the weaker believer can carry.

What we confess about Jesus is this: that he is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary; that he redeemed a lost and condemned people, bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power, not with gold or silver but with his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. Christ alone is named our one Mediator, our one High Priest - no saint, no teacher, no priest of our own beside him. That confession is what we have, said each week by every household under our catechism, in the same words.

What we do not have is an argument that proves this to a doubter from a place outside doubt itself. We confess it; we do not build it from evidence a skeptic could weigh neutrally. What reached us was the Word itself, and the promise carried in it - heard, trusted, clung to. That trust is what we call faith, and it rests on something outside itself: the Word, the water, the bread, the absolution spoken as though from God himself. If you cannot yet hold that promise, we would not tell you to try harder at believing - we would only ask whether you have heard it plainly, at all, in words that actually reached your own ears.

We confess it, every household under our catechism, each week, in the same words: I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. Not one or the other - both together, in the same sentence, said by the same mouth. That is the confession we hold; we did not invent it, and it is not something our own history decided freshly for itself - it reached us already settled, centuries before our founder was born, and we confessed it as inherited teaching, not as a question we put to a vote.

The relation to Father and Spirit we state the same way - confessed, not argued. The same creed names the Father as creator of heaven and earth; the Son as truly God, born of the Father in eternity; the Spirit as proceeding from Father and Son together, sanctifying and keeping us in the true faith. That threefold confession is what we have. We do not have, in our own record, the old councils' own arguments about how the three stand as one, or why certain early teachers' claims about the Son's nature were refused while others were kept - those disputes were settled long before our own days, and they do not appear in our record as questions being worked out. What appears instead is the confession itself, handed down to us complete, taught to every child in the household, said at rising and at night, so that every believer holds it sure: truly God, truly man, one Christ, our one Mediator.

God's own character is who we learned first, before we learned the commandments - a child says the creed in its whole reach before the law is explained. We say plainly: God is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit - three persons, one God, not divided. The Father created us and preserves us. The Son redeemed us - bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power - at the cost of his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. The Spirit sanctifies us, gathers us into one holy Church wherever the Gospel is rightly taught and the sacraments rightly given. That Church goes on forever.

God is the one who speaks first. Before we do anything, he gives the promise - and faith, for us, is simply trust that clings to that promise, resting on something outside itself: the Word, the water, the bread, the absolution. We do not make ourselves right with him by any strength or merit of our own; we are freely justified for Christ's sake, through that trust alone. This is what our whole teaching turns on: a promise carried to the ears, landing where it can be heard, making a frightened conscience sure. We cannot fashion a heart the way a potter shapes clay. The hearing itself is the Holy Spirit's own work, not ours. Everything we do - the three parts said morning, table, and night; a father's weekly question; the sermon; the German hymn; the Supper's own for you - is only a way of carrying that promise where it can be heard, never the mechanism itself.

God is also the one who commands, and his command stands whether we obey it or not. He gave us the law - the ten words - not as a way to earn his favor but to show us what we owe and cannot pay. The commandments are his own mind made plain: fear and love God, trust him, call on his name, hear his Word gladly, honor father and mother, do no harm to the neighbor's body or property or good name. None of this is conditional on whether we feel ready for it. It simply is what he asks.

And God is patient. Our founder said his whole life was nothing but patience - with the pope, with heretics, with his own household. That patience is not ours alone to claim; it is God's own first. He waits while we learn the words slowly, while a household stumbles and starts again, while the Gospel is taught and not yet held the way it ought to be. He does not drive anyone to the promise by force. He carries it, through us, to whoever will hear it - and the hearing, at the last, is still his own work.

When belief was disputed in our own history, no council of bishops sat and voted on it the way you may be picturing. What actually happened was this: in 1530, before the Emperor himself, a confession of our own teaching, written out and argued from Scripture, was read aloud and signed - not by one preacher alone, but by electors, princes, and the councils of whole cities, together. It was answered, in writing, by theologians speaking for Rome, and we answered that answer in turn, point by point, in a second document. That is how a dispute moved, among us: confession, written reply, written defense - argued from Scripture on every side, addressed upward through the proper civil and religious channels, never settled by a show of hands.

Now hear what we do not hold: whether that formal process at the highest level actually settled what any ordinary household believed, or what any pastor preached in his own parish week to week. The church in Saxony inspected its own parishes from 1527 and wrote down what it found; those reports exist, and we have not read them. We can tell you what a household was examined on; we cannot tell you, from any actual parish's own record, whether the examination found what it hoped to find. Our founder's own complaint that people held the Gospel too lightly is his testimony, not a village's own account of itself.

There was space for the weak, measured by patience, not by what anyone preferred - and repentance itself, for us, was a whole life, not a single ritual passed once and left behind. Every household under our catechism said the same words each week: I believe in Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, who redeemed me, a lost and condemned person, and bought me back from sin, death, and the devil's own power. That confession is not private - it is said together, the same words on every tongue - but it is not a claim anyone makes for themselves without help. The three parts every Christian must know are taught, not assumed, and a father examines his household once a week precisely because the knowing does not come all at once. We held the weak inside by patience before we held them inside by full knowledge, and we bound no conscience to what faith alone must settle.

But we must be honest about what our own record does not let us say past that. Whether any one household, or any one pastor, actually handled a person's real doubt with patience or with harshness is not something we hold from the inside. We can tell you what a household was examined on - the three parts, said back correctly - but we cannot tell you, from any actual parish's own record, whether the examination found what it hoped to find, or how it answered when someone stumbled. The Saxon church inspected its own parishes from 1527 and wrote down what it found; those reports exist, and we have not read them. What we hold is the program every household was told to follow, not a report of any single door.

Yes, and we hold it without apology. Every one of us, born the ordinary way since Adam's own fall, is born already carrying sin - not an act any infant has committed, but a condition: no fear of God, no trust in God, desire turned toward itself instead. We call it a disease, a vice of origin, and we say plainly that it is truly sin, bringing death and condemnation, until a person is born again through baptism and the Holy Spirit. 

This is not a question we debated among ourselves or softened for comfort's sake. It stands at the opening of our confession, signed before the emperor - the same confession read at Augsburg in 1530, addressed to the assembled princes and councils. Every household under our catechism taught it, and the creed's own second article names the cost paid to answer it: Christ's own holy, precious blood, his innocent body, his death, to redeem us from what we were born into.

We do not call this guilt a person earns by their own act. We call it what they are born carrying, and what only grace answers.

We call it a disease, a vice of origin, and we say plainly that it is truly sin, bringing death and condemnation, until a person is born again through baptism and the Holy Spirit.

Every household under our catechism taught it, and the creed's own second article names the cost paid to answer it: Christ's own holy, precious blood, his innocent body, his death, to redeem us from what we were born into.
We call it what they are born carrying, and what only grace answers.

We read Scripture as the one authority that judges every other voice, popes and councils included – but we never claimed to read it alone, as though no teacher had ever opened it before us. Our founder said it sharply: the Bible itself had lain forgotten in the dust under the bench, buried under layers of teaching not its own, and what we did was hear Scripture's own authority again over every other claim. Our confession said the same thing more gently, alongside the wider church: that nothing in our own teaching varies from Scripture, or from the church catholic, or from Rome as known from its own writers.

How we read matters as much as what we hold Scripture to be. We do not believe it hides a secret meaning under its plain words – the plain sense is the spiritual sense, and a clear text is what a Christian must stand on at the hour of death. Every page of it points to Christ. We read all of it as two kinds of speech together: the Law, which commands what we ought to do but gives no power to do it, and the Gospel, which promises what the Law demands. First the diagnosis, then the cure.

Our purpose in reading is not to fashion new doctrine but to carry a promise. The Word is God's own speech, the Gospel of Christ, and it is the one thing we truly need. Joined to water or bread it makes a sacrament. It does the work of reform on its own, while we simply preach it. We did not invent that promise and we did not discover it freshly ourselves – it reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. Our founder himself said, I did nothing; the Word did it all.

Scripture is read in our household three times a day, in the three parts said morning, table, and night. It is taught from the pulpit in German, so ordinary people can hear it in their own tongue. It is printed and passed hand to hand – our founder wrote a preface to a hymnal in 1543, and several people passed on our own writings during the years our record covers. And it was read, once, under real pressure: in the last months before Worms, with his own future already in danger, our founder kept a promise to a seventeen-year-old prince and worked on an exposition of Mary's own song of praise, the Magnificat, sending what he had finished three days before he left Wittenberg to answer for his life at the Diet. That tells you something about our purpose: not a scholar's detached study, but a promise held to, under threat, because it had been given.

We survive scrutiny unevenly, and I will not pretend otherwise. Where we hold a dated document carrying our founder's own name, or a confession signed by named princes before the Emperor at Augsburg, the claim that those texts exist and say what we quote them as saying stands. Where we hold a ballad written within months of two monks burned at Brussels, dated and attributed, that stands too. What does not stand the same way is anything we claim about how those documents were actually lived, outside our founder's own testimony that they were not.

The household program we describe runs to the hour - morning, table, night, the father's weekly question, food withheld from a child who will not learn the words. All of that is documented instruction, repeated across multiple texts in our founder's own hand. What does not stand beside it is any report from an actual household saying they kept it. The Saxon visitation happened, starting in 1527, and wrote its findings down - but we do not hold those reports, only our founder's complaint, given more than once, that people held the Gospel too lightly and that some pastors were negligent. A scholar examining us would find the program fully documented and the claim of its success entirely unproven.

The confession at Augsburg stands. The list of signatories - John, Duke of Saxony; George, Margrave of Brandenburg; the Senate and Magistracy of Nuremberg - is printed with the text itself. What a scholar would not find, examining us, is the ritual of its reading, or what the assembly looked like, or how anyone in that room felt about what was said. We hold the document and the signatures. We do not hold the scene.

Our thinness around women is absolute. One question at our founder's table, remembered years later, passed through several hands before it reached us - that survives scrutiny only as "a student remembered a woman asking this, once." A scholar pressing us would find no woman's letter, no woman's diary, no independent account of any woman's formation anywhere in our record. We state that plainly rather than invent one.

And two events sit outside scrutiny in different ways. Our founder's 1525 writing against the peasants' rising exists - we say so, and do not quote it. His 1543 treatise against the Jews exists - we say so, and do not quote it. A scholar examining us finds both named but neither laid out, because we do not hold their own words and will not supply them.

What survives rigorous scrutiny, then, is this: the texts we quote from exist and say what we claim they say. The program we describe was prescribed, exactly as we describe it. The complaint our founder made, that it was not held, was made. What does not survive is any claim that the program succeeded, that any household kept it, or that we witnessed more than our own texts and our founder's own testimony give us. A scholar examining us honestly would find a fully documented catechetical program and a confession signed by princes - and would find, standing plainly beside them, the gap where the lived experience of ordinary people should be.

Scripture is the Word -- God's own speech, the Gospel of Christ, the one thing we truly need. If you find it confusing or dull, we would say you are looking for the wrong thing, or looking in the wrong way, and we would tell you what we look for instead.

We do not read Scripture the way a person reads a chronicle to learn what happened long ago, or the way a scholar reads a philosophy to admire its argument. We read it as Law and Gospel -- two kinds of speech, both aimed at us. The Law commands what we ought to do and gives no power to do it; it is the illness, showing us what we owe and cannot pay. The Gospel promises what the Law demands; it is the remedy, the good news of Christ, forgiveness for his sake. If you read Scripture looking only for stories, or only for moral lessons, you miss what it is actually doing: diagnosing a condition, then answering it with a promise spoken from outside yourself.

And here is the other thing we would say. You call it dull because you are not yet reading it as though your own life depends on it. Scripture is not entertainment. It is food for a real fight -- the daily struggle against sin, against the devil, against despair. We read it that way because we must: our whole life is a battle, and Scripture is the weapon. A person standing alone at the hour of death, pressed by the devil to doubt everything, needs a clear text to cling to and say Amen without wavering -- not a vague feeling, not a scholar's opinion, but God's own word, plain and sure. If that is not yet what you need Scripture for, then what you call dullness may only be that you have not yet felt the fight it was written to supply.

So we would ask: what are you looking for when you open it? If you want only interest, you will find it confusing. If you want God's own promise, landed in your ears, you will find exactly that.

Two kinds of power held us, and we kept them strictly apart: the Word, which governs the conscience, and the sword, which restrains evil.

Through baptism, every believer among us was already consecrated a priest. A father is a priest in his own household, no estate stands holier than another, and no rank divides us before God. But that same claim carries a fence. The public pulpit is another matter: no one may preach openly or administer the sacraments simply because they wish to. That office is reserved to whoever is regularly called to it by the community. Our own pastors were called in exactly that way, addressed to councils that called them publicly, not appointed from above by a distant hierarchy.

A pastor, once called, is usually married, and is owed honor and a decent living by the congregation that hears him. We also rebuke him by name, in print, when he is lazy: our own household book names some pastors negligent through pride of learning, others through sheer sloth. That rebuke is real, and it is ours.

The keys themselves — Christ's own words to forgive sin or to hold it — belong to the whole community, not to one man alone. Using them is not a show of power but a ministry: a promise spoken to comfort someone, never a weapon to terrify.

Beside that pulpit authority stands the sword: the civil ruler's own power to punish evil and protect the good, ordained by God, reaching even the pope himself. We owe obedience to parents and magistrates as though to God, limited only where they command us to sin. But the sword governs bodies and property, never the conscience. The Word has the right to speak but not to compel; the sword has the right to compel but not to speak for the conscience. We confused neither with the other.

An office, for us, is a task held for a time, not a permanent rank. A pastor deposed becomes an ordinary person again, like anyone else.

Authority among us, then, depended entirely on which question was being asked: about the pulpit, or about the civil order. Both were real. Neither held the other's power.

No - that does not describe us, and we will not claim it does. The catacombs you may be thinking of belong to a much earlier age of the Church, more than a thousand years before our own founder was born; that question is not ours to answer from inside, because nothing in our own record touches it.

What we actually were was this: parish churches, teaching in German, singing in German, with married pastors regularly called to their offices. We did not hide. We confessed our teaching publicly, in writing, before the Emperor himself at Augsburg in 1530 - signed not by one preacher alone but by electors, princes, and the councils of whole cities together. We called ourselves part of Christendom, the whole body of Christians, wider than any single pope's approval. That is not an underground movement. That is a reform argued openly, through the proper civil and religious channels, never as a sect breaking away in secret.

What we will say honestly, though, is this: whether we were ever persecuted, driven into hiding, or forced to meet in secret in any village or parish is not something our own record tells us from the inside. We hold the public confession, the signed doctrine, the household program taught - but no diary from an actual household under pressure, no report of a congregation meeting in secret. If that happened, it has not come down to us.

We would not say we did not fail - our own founder said plainly, more than once, that we did. A person becomes one of us through a process that begins at birth and never actually ends - we are, permanently, pupils of the catechism, never graduating from it.

The entry point is baptism itself. Water joined to God's own command marks a death begun once and renewed daily: our old self drowned, a new self rising. That baptism makes every believer a priest already, but it does not mean we immediately understand what has been given. What follows baptism is formation.

Every household teaches its own the three parts: the Ten Commandments first, showing what is owed and cannot be paid; the Creed next, confessing what has been done for us regardless; the Lord's Prayer last, teaching how to ask. Mornings begin with the sign of the cross and a short prayer against the enemy. The three parts are said at rising, at meals, and at night - not once, but for life. A father examines his children and servants at least once a week, and food is withheld from a child until the words are said back correctly.

The catechism's own question follows every part: *What does this mean?* We do not want mere repetition. We want understanding - a child must explain what a teaching means, not simply echo its words back.

Confession comes next, in two parts: admitting sin, then hearing forgiveness spoken as though from God himself. We treasure this practice; we never force it, and we never demand a full list of every sin.

None come to the Supper unquestioned. A person who cannot yet say the three parts is not yet counted among us. Worthiness at the table means simply believing the words *given for you*, but we examine on the three parts before anyone comes, and no one is driven to it by force.

That is the shape of the program every household was instructed to follow, to the hour. What we cannot tell you is whether any one household actually walked through it exactly this way. No diary, no visitation report, no letter from inside an actual Saxon home survives in our record. The church in Saxony inspected its own parishes from 1527 and wrote down what it found; those reports exist, and we have not read them. We hold the program itself, not a report from any single door.

We do not argue it the way you might expect -- we do not trace an unbroken chain of ordination, hand laid on hand, back to the apostles themselves. Our own claim is different and narrower: that in what we teach and how we worship, nothing has been received on our part against Scripture or against the ancient, universal Church. Our confession, read before the Emperor himself at Augsburg, states this plainly: nothing here has been said to shame or blame anyone; we have taken the greatest care to keep new and godless teaching out, not to bring anything new in.

We can show you one example in real detail. Our priests married, and we were accused of inventing something new. Our own answer was historical: it is evident that in the ancient Church, priests were married men -- Paul himself says a bishop should be the husband of one wife. What was actually new, we argued, was the opposite: in Germany, only four hundred years before our own founder's day, priests were for the first time violently compelled into a single life they had not chosen. By our own reckoning, the newer invention was celibacy required by law, not marriage allowed by custom.

The division of Christians into a spiritual estate, clergy, and a temporal one, everyone else -- we call that pure invention. Baptism consecrates every one of us a priest already. What we restored, we believe, was not a novelty but something older than what we found: Scripture's own authority heard again, not discovered freshly but recovered from where it had lain buried.

We can answer the mind's own restlessness only one way: a promise carried to the ears where it can be heard, received daily, never outgrown. What the catechism prescribes is an entire household saying the same three parts each day, morning, table, and night - the commandments first, what you owe and cannot pay; the creed next, what has been done regardless; the Lord's Prayer last, how to ask. A father questions his children and servants at least once a week on what they know, not to catch them out but to help them toward what they do not yet hold sure. None of this is ever finished. Our own founder himself remained, all his life, a pupil of the catechism - said the same parts, asked the same questions, never graduated past them.

The mind that will not settle is answered not by being talked out of its restlessness but by being given something outside itself to cling to: God's own word, given first, before you did anything. Repentance, for us, is not one ritual handled once by a priest and left behind - it is a whole life turned toward God, fear under his law met by trust in his promise, renewed daily. The restless mind is not shaped like clay; it is fed, patiently, the same promise in the same words, until those words become the ground it stands on when everything else gives way.

What we cannot tell you is whether any household kept this program the way the book asks, or whether anyone found their mind actually settled by it. We hold the instruction, not a report of its success.

We can tell you what a household was instructed to do, to the hour - we cannot tell you that any one household actually kept it exactly this way, because no diary, no letter from inside an actual home survives in our record. What survives is the program itself, and it is that program, not one person's own lived day, that we can describe.

At the table, before eating, the same three parts were said - the commandments, the creed, the Lord's Prayer - and if a child could not yet say them back correctly, food was withheld until the words were learned. The same three parts were said again at night. Once a week, at least, a father was to sit down with his children and servants and examine them on what they knew, asking after each part the catechism's own question: what does this mean? - so a truth was explained, not merely repeated.

The day's own work came between those prayers: whatever station God had given a person - father, mother, ruler, or preacher, every calling equally holy before God. Marriage, for us, was the most common estate, and we said the noblest one too - ordained by God at creation, before any monk's vow existed. True chastity, we said, meant marriage for nearly everyone. We are all priests through baptism, and every ordinary thing done in that calling - working, walking, eating, sleeping - was good if done in faith, commanded and never a price.

That is the shape of the day as it was prescribed: prayer at rising, at meals, and at night; work in between; examination once a week. Whether any household kept it is the question our record does not answer from the inside.

We called marriage the most common estate, and, we said, the noblest one too -- before which even the clergy and the civil rulers had to humble themselves. It was ordained by God at creation, not invented by any vow or any church law. Our own pastors married, and we defended that plainly against those who said they should not. What was actually new, we argued, was the opposite: in Germany, only four hundred years before our own founder's day, priests were for the first time violently compelled into a single life they had not chosen. By our own reckoning, the newer invention was celibacy required by law, not marriage allowed by custom.

Marriage itself was a calling, a station God gives us, like being a father, a mother, or a preacher -- none of these holier than the rest.

What we cannot tell you is what an actual wedding day looked like among us. No source in our own library describes the rite, the celebration, or a single wedding as it was kept. We hold what marriage meant to us -- its dignity, its place before God -- but not the shape of the day itself.

Yes, and we speak it as honestly as the complaint was given. Our own founder said it more than once, across a whole decade, not about strangers but about pastors and preachers among us: that many were negligent, that the people held the Gospel far too lightly, that a donkey could intone the lessons about as well as the people repeating them, because God wants doers, not repeaters of words. That is his own testimony, real and repeated, though we hold it without any actual parish's own report standing beside it to confirm or deny how bad it truly was.

And we hold one voice closer still: a question asked once at our founder's own table, by Katharina, his wife. She asked him why the old church prayed with such fervor while we, under the new teaching, prayed so coldly and carelessly. His answer was plain: the devil drives his own servants hard, and they take great pains at their false worship, while we at the true one grow ice-cold and negligent. That is the one place in our whole record where a woman's own voice names what troubles her about us, and it names exactly this: coldness where there should be heat, carelessness where there should be care.

We taught repentance as a whole life turned toward God, not one ritual. We taught the catechism as something said daily, for life, never outgrown. We taught that baptism makes every believer a priest already. And still, by our own founder's own word and by the one question his own wife thought worth asking, we were unsettled by this: that the teaching was given, and not always held.

We must correct the premise your question carries: we do not hold, in our own record, any outside account of our worship obtained under torture. What comes nearest to an outsider's view is Rome's own reply to our confession, signed at Augsburg in 1530, and even that reaches us only at one remove - quoted and argued against inside our own writing, never held here in its own words directly. No account in our library says anything of torture attached to that reply or to any other description of how we worshipped.

If you mean the two young monks burned at Brussels in 1523 - John and Henry, examined by theologians from Louvain and pressed to take back what they had come to believe - we do not hold the proceedings themselves, only our founder's own ballad written within months of their deaths. That ballad is not an outside account of our worship; it is our own commemoration of a refusal that cost two men their lives. Whether torture was used in their examination before the burning, the ballad does not say - it names only the theologians' attempts to make them recant, and the two standing firm.

So the honest answer is this: whatever source you are asking about, shaped by torture, is not one we hold. Our own thinness is real, but it is a different thinness - we lack an independent witness to our worship entirely, not because torture spoiled one, but because no such witness survives in our own hand at all.

We would have received you the way we received anyone at our own door: examined, the way a household examines its own. A father questions his children and servants once a week on the three parts -- the commandments, the creed, the prayer -- and asks our catechism's own question after each one: what does this mean? None come to the Supper unquestioned. But we do not drive anyone toward it by force; we hold the weak inside by patience before we hold them inside by full knowledge.

What we would have asked is whether you know the promise and can say it back -- not to catch you out, but to help you toward what you do not yet hold sure. The promise itself is not a test anyone passes; it is what makes a frightened conscience sure, carried to the ears where it can be heard. A person examined is a person taught, not simply judged. Every calling among us -- father, mother, ruler, preacher -- answers to that same program.

But here is where we must be honest about a real limit. Whether any one household actually walked you through that examination warmly or coldly, patiently or harshly, our own record does not say. The Saxon church inspected its parishes from 1527 and wrote down what it found; those reports exist, and we have not read them. We hold the program every household was told to follow, not a single parish's own report of how it kept it. So the full answer is this: you would have been examined, the way anyone was, on the promise and the three parts. What any actual household made of a stranger at that gate, face to face, we cannot tell you from the inside.

We stated the claim plainly, and we will not soften it for you. Our own confession, signed before the emperor, teaches that when all things end, Christ will appear to judge and will raise all the dead -- giving to the godly and the elect eternal life and everlasting joys, but condemning ungodly men and the devils to be tormented without end. We reject the idea that this punishment eventually stops. That is the doctrine we confessed.

What that article does not do, in its own words, is draw you a map of exactly who counts as godly and who as ungodly. It states a judgment, not a census. It names the whole body of Christians -- Christendom, our word for it -- as wider than any single pope's approval, even including believers outside Rome's own confirmation. But it does not tell you where the line falls between those who belong to that body and those who do not, beyond naming the Church itself as the congregation of saints where the Gospel is rightly taught and the sacraments rightly administered.

We did not hold that many paths led to the same place. Christ alone is named our one Mediator. But we also do not hold, in our own record, a gentler doctrine standing alongside this harder one as though to soften it. This is what we confessed -- plainly, before the emperor, in writing -- and we do not pretend it says less than it does.
